html:
The Zij-i Sultani is the handbook of astronomical tables and star catalogue produced at Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand and finished around 1437 to 1439. It gives the positions of about a thousand stars, with tables for the sun, moon and planets, calendars and trigonometry.

Most earlier Islamic star lists simply updated the catalogue in Ptolemy's Almagest, from the 2nd century, by adding a correction for the slow drift of the stars. Ulugh Beg, finding serious errors in them, had his team measure the stars afresh: the first wholly new catalogue since Ptolemy. Its trigonometric tables, worked out to many decimal places, built on the methods of al-Kashi, who had computed pi to 16 decimal places.

Written in Persian, it was copied and used across the Islamic world. Its accuracy was not surpassed until Taqi al-Din in Istanbul and Tycho Brahe in Denmark in the late 1500s. Oxford scholars printed parts of it in Latin in the 1600s. It marks the late peak of the science that flourished under the Timurids.
